content: Old age refers to the stage of life that approaches or surpasses the average human lifespan, marking the final phase of the human life cycle. In the United States, older individuals are often referred to as seniors or elderly. There is a belief that Western cultures harbor prejudice against older individuals, a form of discrimination known as ageism. Physiologically, older adults experience reduced regenerative capacity and are more susceptible to diseases, syndromes, and illnesses compared to younger adults. The biological study of aging is termed senescence, while the medical field dedicated to understanding the aging process is called gerontology. The branch of medicine that focuses on diseases affecting the elderly is known as geriatrics. The transition from middle age to old age is not universally defined, as its meaning varies across cultures and societies. In many regions, individuals are considered old based on changes in their social roles or activities. For instance, becoming a grandparent or retiring from work may signify old age. In the United States and Europe, chronological age often determines this classification. Many Americans associate the age of 65 with the onset of old age, as this is when individuals become eligible for full Social Security benefits. Those aged 65 and older are frequently referred to as senior citizens. However, starting in 2003, the age for full Social Security eligibility began to gradually increase, and by 2027, it will reach 67 years. Stereotypes about older adults are common and include assumptions such as reliance on walking aids, frequent medical visits, and excessive sleep. These generalizations are often inaccurate and unfair. Many older individuals maintain mobility and independence, although certain illnesses are more prevalent in this age group. Globally, the population of individuals aged 65 and older is growing at an unprecedented rate, particularly in developed nations. In the United States, the proportion of people aged 65 or older increased from 4% in 1900 to approximately 13% by the late 1990s. In 1900, only about 3 million Americans had reached the age of 65, but by 1998, this number had risen to approximately 34 million. Demographic experts predict that by 2020, over 50 million Americans—roughly 17% of the population—will be 65 or older. This global increase in the elderly population is largely attributed to higher survival rates into adulthood. Life expectancy differs between genders, with women generally living longer than men. In the United States during the late 1990s, the average life expectancy at birth was 80 years for women and 77 years for men. Women who reached the age of 65 during this period could expect to live an additional 19 years on average, while men of the same age could anticipate an additional 16 years.
